When stationary charged bodies are described in terms of local interactions, their electrostatic interaction energy can be attributed to the electric field.
If a dielectric is present, this description of stored energy also includes the energy associated with reversible polarization of the dielectric;

it is not the sum of all the energy of the charged bodies.
For an appropriate model of the dielectric, the stored energy can be expressed in terms of the electric field's main property: its field strength.

First consider an ideal parallel-plate capacitor: neglect fringing effects so that the electric field between the plates is approximately uniform.
The space between the plates is either a vacuum or a homogeneous, linear, isotropic, nondispersive dielectric with negligible losses;

the properties of the dielectric and the geometry of the plates remain fixed.

For an alternating electric field, under the same dielectric conditions, the instantaneous field strength can be used to calculate the instantaneous stored energy density of the electric-field part.
An alternating electromagnetic field may also store energy in its magnetic field. The magnetic-field part must be calculated separately;

the electric-field expressions above must not be treated as the total electromagnetic-field energy.
These two expressions cannot be applied directly to a dielectric that is dispersive or nonlinear, or has significant losses.
